days.title: Classification & Taxonomy
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define taxonomy and systematics.
  • Describe the hierarchical classification system.
  • Apply binomial nomenclature.
  • Explain the 3-domain and 5-kingdom schemes.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Taxonomy — science of naming and classifying organisms.
  • Systematics — study of evolutionary relationships.
  • Binomial nomenclature — two-part naming (Genus species).
  • Domain — largest taxonomic rank.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Hierarchical Classification

Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species

B. Binomial Nomenclature

  • Developed by Linnaeus
  • Genus capitalized, species lowercase
  • Both italicized
  • Example: Homo sapiens

C. Classification Schemes

SchemeGroups
3-DomainBacteria, Archaea, Eukarya
5-KingdomMonera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia

D. Why 3-Domain is Preferred

Molecular evidence (rRNA) shows Archaea and Bacteria are fundamentally different.

💬 Let's Discuss

Scientists have named about 2 million species, and millions more are still undescribed. To organize them, biologists use taxonomy, the science of naming, describing and classifying organisms. Systematics goes further: it classifies organisms according to their evolutionary relationships.

In the 1700s, the Swedish botanist Carolus Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature, a two-part scientific name: Genus + species. Rules: write it in italics (or underline it when handwritten), capitalize the genus only, and keep the species epithet lowercase — Homo sapiens, Oryza sativa (rice), Pithecophaga jefferyi (Philippine eagle). Common names change from place to place (a "kalabaw" or "water buffalo"), but scientific names are the same worldwide.

Linnaeus also created a hierarchy of ranks from broadest to most specific: Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species (memory aid: Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup). Humans are Eukarya, Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, Homo, sapiens.

Classification systems change as knowledge grows. The five-kingdom system (Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia) grouped all prokaryotes in Monera. In 1990, Carl Woese used rRNA sequences to show that prokaryotes are actually two very different groups, giving the three-domain system: Bacteria and Archaea (both prokaryotic) and Eukarya (all eukaryotes). So "Monera" is no longer used.

Common mistake: writing Homo Sapiens or homo sapiens. Only the genus is capitalized, and both words are italicized.

pairs.why: Taxonomy is the science of naming and classifying organisms.
Systematics studies the evolutionary relationships among organisms.
Binomial nomenclature uses genus + species.
Domain is the broadest taxonomic rank.
The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.
The five-kingdom system has Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

scenarios.explanation: Genus capitalized, species lowercase, both italicized.

scenarios.explanation: Domain is the largest rank.

scenarios.explanation: Bacteria and Archaea are prokaryotic domains.

scenarios.explanation: Monera was split into Bacteria and Archaea, so it is not used in the 3-domain scheme.

scenarios.explanation: Species is the most specific rank.

scenarios.explanation: Humans are animals, chordates, mammals and primates.

questions.explanation: Correct form: Homo sapiens, italicized, genus capitalized.

questions.text: Which domains are in the 3-domain system?
questions.explanation: The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya.

takeaways: Taxonomy names & classifies; systematics studies relationships.
Hierarchy: Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
3-Domain is preferred based on molecular evidence.

days.title: Taxa & Distinctive Characteristics
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define taxon.
  • Identify distinctive characteristics of major taxa.
  • Compare members of different kingdoms.
  • Explain how DNA helps classify organisms.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Taxon — any group at any taxonomic level.
  • Distinctive characteristics — features that distinguish a taxon.
  • Molecular taxonomy — uses DNA sequences.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Major Kingdoms

KingdomDistinctive Features
Monera (Bacteria/Archaea)Prokaryotic, no nucleus
ProtistaEukaryotic, mostly unicellular
FungiEukaryotic, chitin cell walls, heterotrophic
PlantaeEukaryotic, cellulose cell walls, autotrophic
AnimaliaEukaryotic, no cell wall, heterotrophic, motile

B. Structural vs Molecular Classification

  • Structural — physical features (morphology)
  • Developmental — embryology
  • Molecular — DNA/protein sequences

C. Example

Some organisms that look similar are genetically very different (convergent evolution), and vice versa.

💬 Let's Discuss

A taxon (plural taxa) is any named group at any rank — the genus Mangifera, the class Mammalia and the kingdom Fungi are all taxa. Each kingdom is defined by a few distinctive characteristics; learn these and you can place almost any organism.

Monera (Bacteria and Archaea): prokaryotic — no nucleus; mostly unicellular; many have cell walls (peptidoglycan in bacteria). Examples: E. coli, Lactobacillus, archaea in hot springs. Protista: mostly unicellular eukaryotes, a very mixed group — animal-like (amoeba, Plasmodium which causes malaria), plant-like (algae, diatoms) and fungus-like (slime molds). Fungi: eukaryotes with cell walls made of chitin; heterotrophs that absorb nutrients after digesting food outside their bodies; decomposers. Examples: mushrooms, yeast, molds. Plantae: multicellular eukaryotes with cell walls of cellulose, chloroplasts and autotrophic nutrition by photosynthesis. Examples: mosses, ferns, rice, narra. Animalia: multicellular eukaryotes with no cell wall; heterotrophs that ingest food; most can move at some stage.

Appearance can mislead. Dolphins look like fish, but they breathe air and nurse their young — they are mammals. Similar body shapes in unrelated groups result from convergent evolution under similar conditions. That is why modern classification relies heavily on DNA sequences and other homologous traits rather than outward appearance.

Common mistake: putting mushrooms in the plant kingdom. Fungi do not photosynthesize and have chitin walls; they are more closely related to animals than to plants.

pairs.why: A taxon is any named group at any rank.
Monera includes prokaryotes.
Most protists are single-celled eukaryotes.
Fungi have cell walls made of chitin.
Plants have cellulose cell walls and make their own food.
Animals lack cell walls and must eat other organisms.

scenarios.text: Organism has chitin cell walls and is heterotrophic.
scenarios.explanation: Chitin walls plus heterotrophic nutrition means Fungi.

scenarios.text: Organism has cellulose cell walls and photosynthesizes.
scenarios.explanation: Cellulose walls plus photosynthesis means Plantae.

scenarios.text: Organism has no cell wall and moves.
scenarios.explanation: No cell wall and able to move means Animalia.

scenarios.text: Organism is prokaryotic.
scenarios.explanation: Prokaryotic organisms belong to Monera (Bacteria/Archaea).

scenarios.text: Unicellular eukaryote.
scenarios.explanation: A single-celled eukaryote is usually a protist.

scenarios.text: Two organisms look alike but are genetically different.
scenarios.explanation: Look-alikes that are not closely related result from convergent evolution.

questions.text: Which kingdom has NO cell wall?
Which is used to classify organisms by evolutionary relationships?

takeaways: Taxa are groups at any taxonomic level.
Structural, developmental, and molecular data help classify organisms.
Molecular data can reveal hidden relationships.

days.title: Species Diversity & Cladistics
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define species diversity.
  • Explain cladistics.
  • Differentiate ancestral from derived traits.
  • Identify shared derived characteristics.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Species diversity — variety of species in an ecosystem.
  • Cladistics — grouping by shared derived characteristics.
  • Ancestral trait — primitive trait shared with distant ancestors.
  • Derived trait — new trait unique to a group.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Species Diversity

  • Species richness — number of species
  • Species evenness — how evenly distributed
  • Highest in tropical rainforests

B. Cladistics

Groups organisms based on shared derived characteristics (synapomorphies). A clade includes an ancestor and all its descendants.

C. Trait Types

Trait TypeMeaning
Ancestral (plesiomorphy)Old trait, shared broadly
Derived (apomorphy)New trait, unique to a group
SynapomorphyShared derived trait

💬 Let's Discuss

Species diversity describes the variety of species in an area, and it has two parts. Species richness is simply the number of different species. Species evenness is how equally individuals are distributed among those species. Two forests may each have 10 tree species (same richness), but if one forest is 91% narra and only 1% each of the others, it is less even — and less diverse — than a forest where each species makes up 10%. Diversity is highest in tropical rainforests and coral reefs; the Philippines is one of the world's 17 megadiverse countries, with many endemic species found nowhere else.

To classify this diversity by evolutionary history, biologists use cladistics, which groups organisms by shared derived characters. An ancestral character is an old trait inherited from a distant ancestor and shared widely — a backbone is ancestral for all vertebrates. A derived character is a newer trait that evolved in a particular lineage — hair and milk are derived characters of mammals. A shared derived character is called a synapomorphy, and it defines a clade (an ancestor plus all its descendants).

Whether a trait is ancestral or derived depends on the group you are studying. Within mammals, a backbone is ancestral because all of them have it, so it tells you nothing about relationships among mammals. Hair, on the other hand, separates mammals from reptiles.

Common mistake: grouping organisms by traits that everyone in the group shares (ancestral traits) or by traits that evolved separately (like wings in bats and birds). Only shared derived homologous traits reveal clades.

pairs.why: Species diversity is the variety of species in an area.
Species richness counts the number of species.
Species evenness describes how equally individuals are spread among species.
Cladistics groups organisms by shared derived traits.
An ancestral trait is old and widely shared.
A derived trait is newer and found in a particular group.
A synapomorphy is a derived trait shared by members of a clade.

scenarios.text: An ecosystem has 500 species.
scenarios.explanation: Many species present means high species richness.

scenarios.text: A trait is unique to mammals.
scenarios.explanation: A trait unique to mammals is derived.

scenarios.text: A trait is shared by all vertebrates.
scenarios.explanation: A trait shared by all vertebrates is ancestral among vertebrates.

scenarios.text: Grouping organisms by shared derived traits.
scenarios.explanation: Grouping by shared derived traits is cladistics.

scenarios.text: A clade includes:
scenarios.explanation: A clade is an ancestor plus all its descendants.

scenarios.text: Highest species diversity is in:
scenarios.explanation: Tropical rainforests have the highest species diversity.

questions.explanation: Species richness is the number of species.
Cladistics groups organisms by shared derived characters.
A synapomorphy is a shared derived trait.

takeaways: Cladistics groups by shared derived traits.

days.title: Building & Interpreting Cladograms
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Construct a simple cladogram.
  • Interpret nodes and branches.
  • Identify monophyletic groups.
  • Compare cladistics with traditional taxonomy.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Cladogram — branching diagram of relationships.
  • Node — common ancestor point.
  • Monophyletic group — ancestor + all descendants.
  • Outgroup — reference taxon outside the study group.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Constructing a Cladogram

  1. Choose the group of interest
  2. Choose an outgroup
  3. Identify shared derived traits
  4. Group by shared derived traits

B. Reading a Cladogram

  • Nodes = common ancestors
  • Branches = lineages
  • Tips = species or groups
  • Character changes marked on branches

C. Example

Vertebrate cladogram: Fish → Amphibians → Reptiles → Birds → Mammals. Traits: jaws, lungs, amniotic egg, feathers, hair.

💬 Let's Discuss

A cladogram is a branching diagram that shows the order in which groups evolved their derived traits. Building one is like solving a puzzle.

Step 1: choose the ingroup (the organisms you are studying) and an outgroup — a related organism outside the group, used as a reference. Any trait the outgroup lacks is considered derived within the ingroup. Step 2: make a character table: list traits and mark which organisms have each. Step 3: sort organisms by how many derived traits they share; the trait shared by the most organisms appeared earliest. Step 4: draw the diagram. Each node is a common ancestor; mark each new trait on the branch where it first appears; organisms above that mark have the trait, those below do not.

Example (vertebrates): outgroup lancelet (no backbone). Traits: vertebrae (all vertebrates) → jaws (sharks and above) → bony skeleton/lungs or lung derivatives (bony fish and above) → four limbs (amphibians and above) → amniotic egg (reptiles, birds, mammals) → hair and milk (mammals only). A frog has vertebrae, jaws and four limbs but no amniotic egg, so it branches off before reptiles.

A monophyletic group (a true clade) includes an ancestor and all its descendants. A paraphyletic group leaves some descendants out — "reptiles" without birds is paraphyletic, which is why many biologists now place birds within reptiles.

Common mistake: thinking that organisms at the top of a cladogram are "more evolved." The diagram shows branching order, not superiority.

pairs.why: A cladogram is a branching diagram of shared derived traits.
Each node represents a common ancestor.
A monophyletic group includes an ancestor and all its descendants.
The outgroup is used as a reference for identifying derived traits.
Each new trait is marked where it first appears on the branches.
